docs.text:
Independent project · Autonomous driving · Nov 2026

The car slows for a crosswalk it cannot see, before anyone appears.

"My view of the crosswalk 11 m ahead is blocked by T1; limiting speed to 5.3 m/s so I can stop if someone steps out." The car slows before it can see anyone. When the pedestrian appears from behind the truck, it stops comfortably. The reactive baseline in the same scene hits the pedestrian.

docs.title: ExplainDrive: An Explainable Reasoning Planner
docs.text:
A small, fully inspectable driving stack that reasons about a scene, plans a path, says why in plain English, and checks that those explanations are true.

Pure Python (NumPy, Matplotlib). No GPU, no CARLA, no datasets. Every result regenerates with one command.

Motion planningFrenet plannerExplainable AIClosed-loop simPython

Scenarios & results Design notes View source files

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Recent "reasoning" driving models plan a path and explain their decisions. ExplainDrive builds the same reason → plan → explain loop from first principles, small enough for one engineer to understand, test and measure end to end:

  • a scene reasoner that turns what the car sees into driving constraints and the reasons for them,
  • a Frenet sampling trajectory planner that drives inside those constraints,
  • a closed-loop simulator with occlusion-aware perception, a kinematic bicycle model and 6 hard scenarios,
  • and four experiments a reasoning model should face: baseline comparison, adaptive (fast/slow) reasoning, latency sensitivity for edge hardware, and explanation faithfulness checked with counterfactuals.
flowchart LR
  P[Perception<br/>occlusion-aware] --> L[Latency buffer]
  L --> R[Scene reasoner<br/>constraints + rationale]
  R --> PL[Frenet sampling planner]
  PL --> C[Pure pursuit + speed control]
  C --> W[World: kinematic bicycle]
  W --> P
  R --> X[Plain-English explanation]
  X --> F[Faithfulness check<br/>counterfactual deletion]

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text: This document explains how each layer works and why it was built that way. The README covers results and usage.

docs.title: 1. Loop timing
docs.text:
The simulator runs at 10 Hz (dt = 0.1 s). Every tick:

  1. Perception (perception.py) takes the true world state and returns what the ego can see. An agent is visible if any of its sample points (centre plus 4 corners, or the centre only for pedestrians) has a clear line of sight from the front bumper, within 150 m. It also checks 9 points on the right curb at each crosswalk ahead. If any of them is hidden, it records an OccludedArea with the id of the blocking object.
  2. Latency buffer. The stack does not see the newest observation. It sees the one from latency seconds ago. The plan it produces is then tracked from that older time origin, so a 300 ms latency means the controller is always following a plan made from a 300 ms old world.
  3. Reasoning (reasoning.py) turns the observation into a Decision, which holds a maneuver, Constraints and a list of Rationale. With the adaptive policy, this step is skipped on calm ticks and the cached decision is reused.
  4. Planning (planner.py) samples trajectories inside the constraints, checks them against predictions and picks the cheapest. It runs every tick even when reasoning is skipped, which keeps collision checking always fresh.
  5. Control (control.py) uses pure pursuit for steering and feed-forward plus P control for speed.
  6. Physics (world.py) is a kinematic bicycle model about the centre of gravity, with limits on steering angle, steering rate and acceleration. All other agents follow their scripted behaviours.
  7. Metrics run on the ground truth: collisions use the separating-axis theorem on the true polygons, and clearances use the true polygons too.

docs.title: 2. The reasoner: constraints, not trajectories
docs.text:
The reasoner never outputs a path. It outputs:

field meaning v_max speed cap (a target, and a hard limit after a short comfort ramp) stop_x the front bumper must stay behind this x y_lo, y_hi allowed lateral corridor for the ego centre y_pref preferred lateral position lead_id vehicle to keep a safe following gap to

Each rule writes into these fields and adds a Rationale(rule, maneuver, agent_ids, text). When rules are combined, the tightest value wins (minimum speed cap, earliest stop line, intersection of corridors), and the reported maneuver is the one with the highest priority:

EMERGENCY > YIELD > WAIT > NUDGE = OVERTAKE > CAUTION > FOLLOW > CRUISE

Keeping the reasoner's output small and structured is what makes the explanations testable. Each explanation names specific agents, and each constraint can be traced back to the rule that set it.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
rule trigger effect lead same-direction vehicle in the corridor ahead v_max = v_lead + (gap - (s0 + T·v)) / 2, plus lead_id cut_in adjacent vehicle whose lateral velocity carries it into the corridor within 2 s same as lead, raised earlier crosswalk pedestrian on the road at a crosswalk who hasn't cleared our lane, or one stepping off the curb stop_x = 1 m before the crosswalk (only if stopping needs ≤ 7 m/s²) curb pedestrian standing at the curb by a crosswalk v_max = max(6, v_stop(d)) occlusion crosswalk entry hidden by an object v_max = max(3, v_stop(d)), citing the blocker oncoming_nudge oncoming vehicle whose near edge leaves less than 0.6 m of clearance corridor shifted right onto the shoulder, v_max = 7 within 50 m oncoming_block no room at all pull right and stop overtake_sight parked obstacle in lane, but the oncoming lane can't be seen far enough (range limit or the obstacle itself) stop 10 m behind, edge left to look past it overtake_wait parked obstacle, and an oncoming vehicle reaches the passing zone before t_need + 2.5 s stop behind it overtake parked obstacle and the gap is clear corridor widened into the oncoming lane, y_pref = oncoming lane centre until passed

v_stop(d) is the highest speed from which the car can stop within d metres, allowing for a reaction time: it solves v·t_r + v²/(2a) = d with t_r = 1 s and a = 3 m/s². Without the reaction-time term, the car always arrived about 0.8 s "late" to its own speed cap and needed emergency braking when the pedestrian appeared. Simulation runs caught this.

Overtaking keeps a little memory: once the ego has started to pull out, it stays committed, unless it hasn't yet left its own lane, in which case it can still abort.

docs.title: 3. The planner
docs.text:
The planner follows the Frenet sampling idea from Werling et al. (2010). On a straight road, (s, d) = (x, y).

  • Longitudinal: quartic velocity-keeping profiles to v_max × {1, .75, .5, .25, 0} over T ∈ {1.5, 3, 5} s. When a stop line is active, it adds quintic stop-at-position profiles and one constant-deceleration "brake to the line" profile.
  • Lateral: quintic in distance travelled, d(s), toward each of up to 6 target offsets (5 spread across the corridor plus y_pref), over lengths max(v·T, L_min). The first version used d(t). It asked for sideways motion that a car can't make at walking speed, and overtakes from a standstill failed because the bicycle model couldn't follow. Planning d(s) makes every candidate drivable by construction.
  • Feasibility checks (vectorised over all candidates × all time steps): no reversing; a ∈ [-6, 2.5]; heading slope |dy/dx| ≤ 0.7; curvature ≤ min(κ_steer, a_lat,max / v²); stay inside the corridor or move steadily back into it; speed cap with a 0.8 s ramp; stop line, including the requirement that the car can still stop after the horizon ends (x_end + v_end²/2a ≤ stop_x); and collisions.
  • Collision model: the ego is 4 circles along its heading, and every other agent is an oriented rectangle moving along its predicted path. The margins are 0.3 m laterally and 1.0 m longitudinally for vehicles, and 0.8 m for pedestrians. If the ego is already inside the margin, for example while squeezing past a bus, a candidate is rejected only if it gets closer.
  • Cost: lateral and longitudinal jerk, lateral acceleration, distance from the target speed, distance from y_pref, longitudinal acceleration, an exponential proximity penalty and corridor violation.
  • Fallback: if nothing is feasible, the planner brakes at -8 m/s² in a straight line. The reasons candidates were rejected become the emergency explanation, for example "every comfortable trajectory comes too close to S1".

docs.title: 4. Explanations and faithfulness
docs.text:
An explanation event is logged only when the pair (maneuver, primary rule, cited agents) changes and the new decision has lasted 3 ticks. Emergencies are logged immediately. This keeps explanations "when needed": a whole scenario produces 2–5 sentences, not 150.

faithfulness.py checks each event against counterfactual scenes, using the same reasoner state and the same observation:

  • necessity: removing each cited agent must change the decision materially (the maneuver, or any constraint by more than 0.5 m/s, 0.2 m or 1 m);
  • completeness: removing each uncited visible agent must not change it.

This test caught a real bug. In the stalled-car scenario, the wait message cited the oncoming car C1. But the ego could not have passed anyway, because it couldn't see far enough down the oncoming lane, so removing C1 changed nothing. The decision was overdetermined, and the explanation blamed the wrong thing. The fix was to cite only the binding reason (the limited view) and mention C1 in the text without citing it.

docs.title: 5. Adaptive ("fast/slow") reasoning
docs.text:
scene_complexity() is a cheap score computed every tick from the number, type and closing speed of nearby agents and from occlusions. The full reasoner runs when:

  • the complexity is at least 3, or
  • the complexity has changed by at least 1 since the last run, or
  • 1 s has passed since the last run.

Otherwise the last decision is reused. The planner still runs every tick, so collision checking is never stale. The comparison experiment measures how many reasoner calls this saves and whether it costs anything in collisions, emergency braking or comfort.

docs.title: 6. LLM/VLM plug-in
docs.text: llm_reasoner.GuardedLLMReasoner writes the observation out as text and asks any prompt -> str backend for JSON. It then merges that answer with the rule-based decision so the more cautious value wins on every field. The model can add caution (a lower speed or an earlier stop) and choose a position inside the rule-based corridor. It can never widen the envelope. If the output can't be parsed, the reasoner falls back to the rules alone. This is the slot for comparing an open model against the rules under identical scenarios.

docs.title: 7. Known simplifications
docs.text:
• The road is straight and there are no junctions. Curved roads would need a proper Frenet transform.
  • Perception is perfect inside line of sight: there is no noise, no false positives and no tracking.
  • Other agents follow scripts and don't react to the ego. Because of this, the reactive-baseline "bus collisions" partly come from a bus driver who never moves over.
  • Prediction is constant velocity. The reactive baseline ignores lateral velocity (it assumes lane keeping).
  • Planner runtimes are for Python and NumPy on a laptop-class CPU. They show relative cost, not embedded performance.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
scenario what makes it hard reasoning planner pedestrian_crosswalk a pedestrian steps off the curb yields at the stop line until they clear its lane oncoming_bus a 2.55 m wide bus drifts 0.8 m over the centre line of a narrow road shifts 0.9 m onto the shoulder and slows to 7 m/s stalled_car a broken-down car blocks the lane while oncoming traffic arrives waits, edges left to see, then overtakes in the gap cut_in a slower car cuts in 12 m ahead spots the lateral motion early and rebuilds the gap occluded_crosswalk a parked truck hides a running pedestrian slows because of the occlusion, before it sees anyone lead_brake the lead car brakes hard to a stop, then pulls away follows with a safe gap (a sanity check)

Each scenario also takes a random seed (make(name, seed)) that varies timings, speeds and positions, which is what the experiments use.

The animations show the green corridor the reasoner allows, a red stop line when one is active, the chosen plan (green) and other candidate plans (faint), agents the ego cannot see (dashed), and the object blocking the view (purple outline). Below the road are the current explanation and the speed against the reasoner's speed cap.

Baseline runs for comparison: bus, occluded crosswalk, stalled car.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: All numbers come from python scripts/make_media.py (seeded, deterministic). Raw JSON is in results/.

docs.title: 1. Does reasoning help? (reactive vs reasoning vs adaptive, 10 randomised seeds per scenario)
docs.text:
The reactive baseline is a typical ACC-plus-lane-keeping stack. It uses the same planner and the same collision checking, but it has no crosswalk, occlusion, nudging, overtaking or cut-in logic, and it assumes other cars stay in their lane.

scenario policy collisions completed runs with emergency braking min clearance [m] RMS jerk [m/s³] reasoner calls/s pedestrian_crosswalk reactive 0% 100% 20% 0.86 4.07 10.1 pedestrian_crosswalk reasoning 0% 100% 0% 3.62 3.55 10.1 pedestrian_crosswalk adaptive 0% 100% 0% 3.63 3.60 7.6 oncoming_bus reactive 100% 0% 100% 0.01 9.13 10.1 oncoming_bus reasoning 0% 100% 0% 0.71 2.86 10.1 oncoming_bus adaptive 0% 100% 0% 0.71 2.85 1.1 stalled_car reactive 0% 0% 100% 1.60 1.26 10.0 stalled_car reasoning 0% 100% 0% 0.92 1.71 10.1 stalled_car adaptive 0% 100% 0% 0.92 1.75 5.5 cut_in reactive 10% 90% 30% 0.21 3.55 10.1 cut_in reasoning 0% 100% 20% 1.60 2.85 10.0 cut_in adaptive 0% 100% 10% 1.56 2.83 1.1 occluded_crosswalk reactive 70% 30% 100% 0.00 10.67 10.2 occluded_crosswalk reasoning 0% 100% 0% 0.91 3.67 10.1 occluded_crosswalk adaptive 0% 100% 0% 0.84 4.35 5.7 lead_brake reactive 0% 100% 0% 12.43 2.00 10.1 lead_brake reasoning 0% 100% 0% 12.43 2.00 10.1 lead_brake adaptive 0% 100% 0% 10.11 2.52 1.6

Across all 6 scenarios × 10 seeds, the reasoning planner had a 0% collision rate and completed 100% of runs. The reactive baseline collided in 30% and completed 53%.

The baseline's failures are exactly where scene reasoning is needed:

  • oncoming_bus: it collides in 10 of 10 runs. It stays in its lane and brakes, but braking alone cannot get it out of the way of a bus that is over the line.
  • occluded_crosswalk: it collides in 7 of 10 runs. It reaches the hidden crosswalk at full speed and sees the pedestrian too late to stop.
  • stalled_car: it never collides, but it never finishes either. It waits behind the broken-down car forever.
  • cut_in: it collides in 1 of 10 runs. Because it assumes cars stay in their lanes, it notices the cut-in late.

On the two sanity scenarios (pedestrian_crosswalk and lead_brake), both stacks are safe. That is expected, since the shared planner's collision checking covers simple cases. Even so, the baseline needed emergency braking for the pedestrian in 2 of 10 runs, while the reasoning planner yielded early and never did.

The reasoning planner is not perfect: it needed emergency braking in 2 of 10 cut-in runs. In those seeds the car cuts in closer than the comfortable braking limits can handle, but it still never collided.

docs.title: 2. Adaptive "fast/slow" reasoning
docs.text:
Reasoning models are expensive, and on an edge computer you would not want to run one every 100 ms in an empty street. The adaptive policy runs a cheap scene-complexity score every tick. It calls the full reasoner only when the scene is complex, when the scene has just changed, or once per second as a heartbeat. The planner and its collision checks still run every tick.

full reasoning every tick adaptive reasoner calls per simulated second (mean over scenarios) 10.1 3.8 collision rate 0% 0% runs needing emergency braking 3.3% 1.7% mean RMS jerk [m/s³] 2.77 2.98

The adaptive policy cuts reasoner calls by 63% with no collisions and no extra emergency braking. Its cost is a slightly less smooth ride (+8% RMS jerk), because it reacts to a slowing lead car up to one heartbeat late. On the oncoming bus it calls the reasoner 14 times instead of 119. On an edge computer, that compute budget could go to a much larger model that runs only when the scene needs it.

docs.title: 3. How much latency can the stack take?
docs.text:
The whole perception → reasoning → planning chain is delayed, so the car acts on a world that is up to 800 ms old, as it would with a large model on a slow embedded GPU.

latency collision rate runs with emergency braking min pedestrian clearance [m] min vehicle clearance [m] mean peak decel [m/s²] collisions by scenario 0 ms 0% 7% 3.28 0.71 5.28 none 100 ms 0% 23% 2.03 0.73 5.66 none 200 ms 0% 20% 1.68 0.73 5.52 none 300 ms 0% 27% 1.46 0.73 5.82 none 500 ms 0% 27% 1.23 0.73 6.59 none 800 ms 7% 50% 0.21 0.32 7.53 cut_in: 1, occluded_crosswalk: 1

The stack stays collision-free up to 500 ms of end-to-end latency. Latency still costs something: the minimum pedestrian clearance shrinks from 3.3 m to 1.2 m, peak braking rises, and emergency braking becomes more common. At 800 ms the first collisions appear, in the cut-in and the occluded-pedestrian scenarios, which are the two where a hazard appears suddenly. Together these give a concrete latency budget for an on-vehicle reasoning model: under about 300 ms keeps the margins comfortable, and more than about 500 ms is unsafe for this scenario set.

docs.title: 4. Are the explanations true?
docs.text:
An explanation that names the wrong cause is worse than none. For every explanation, faithfulness.py re-runs the reasoner on the same scene with one agent deleted:

  • necessity: deleting an agent the explanation cites must change the decision;
  • completeness: deleting an agent it does not cite must not change the decision.

Over every explanation in 5 seeds × 6 scenarios, the test ran 71 cited-agent and 79 uncited-agent counterfactuals. Necessity was 100% and completeness was 100%: every agent the car blamed actually mattered, and nothing it left out did. Emergency stops come from the planner rather than the reasoner, so they are explained by the planner's rejection reasons and are not part of this test.

This check found a real bug during development. In the stalled-car scene, the "waiting" explanation blamed the oncoming car. But the ego could not see far enough down the oncoming lane anyway, so deleting that car changed nothing. The decision was overdetermined and the explanation picked the wrong cause. The fix was to cite only the binding reason and mention the other one in the text without citing it. See docs/design.md.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    W[World<br/>scripted agents] -->|ground truth| P[Perception<br/>line of sight, occlusions]
    P --> B[(latency buffer)]
    B --> S{complexity<br/>gate}
    S -->|complex or changed| R[Scene reasoner<br/>rules → constraints + reasons]
    S -->|calm| C[cached decision]
    R --> PL
    C --> PL[Sampling planner<br/>Frenet quintics, collision checks]
    PL --> CT[Tracker<br/>pure pursuit + speed loop]
    CT --> V[Bicycle model]
    V --> W
    R -.-> E[Explanation events<br/>when the decision changes]
    E -.-> F[Faithfulness<br/>counterfactual check]

The reasoner outputs constraints, not trajectories. Each rule writes a speed cap, a stop line, a lateral corridor, a preferred offset or a lead vehicle, and attaches a Rationale that names the agents it depends on. The tightest constraint wins, and the highest-priority maneuver is the one reported. Because of this split, every explanation is grounded in a specific, checkable constraint, and the planner can be swapped or tested independently.

The planner samples quintic lateral paths in distance travelled (so they are drivable even when pulling out from a standstill) and quartic or quintic speed profiles. It rejects anything that breaks acceleration, curvature, corridor, speed-cap or stop-line limits, or that comes within a margin of any predicted agent. It then picks the cheapest of the rest by jerk, lateral acceleration, speed error, offset and proximity. If nothing is feasible it brakes as hard as it can and explains which constraint made every option fail.

The LLM/VLM slot. llm_reasoner.py writes the scene out as text, asks any prompt → str backend for a JSON decision, and merges it with the rules so that the more cautious value always wins. A model can add caution or choose a position inside the safe corridor, but it can never widen the safety envelope. Unparseable output falls back to the rules alone.

The full details are in docs/design.md: equations, every rule, the planner checks, and the bugs simulation exposed along the way.
